content: The analysis of the data reveals the following findings: 1. There was no significant difference observed between ASPY and AL in terms of the specified outcome, and therefore, no downgrade was applied for imprecision. However, in this update, a reduced rate was reported in the ASPY group. Since a potential difference was identified, a downgrade for imprecision was applied. 2. ASPY may result in fewer PCR-adjusted failures at day 28 compared to AL. This conclusion is based on data from 2,575 participants across four randomized controlled trials. The difference was estimated at 3 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 12 fewer to 12 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 3. There may be little or no difference in PCR-adjusted failures at day 42 between ASPY and AL. This conclusion is based on data from 3,149 participants across four randomized controlled trials. The difference was estimated at 92 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 110 fewer to 53 fewer). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and inconsistency. The inclusion of additional data in this review increased heterogeneity among the trials. 4. ASPY may result in fewer unadjusted failures at day 28 compared to AL. This conclusion is based on data from 3,080 participants across four randomized controlled trials. The difference was estimated at 99 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 137 fewer to 46 fewer). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious inconsistency and indirectness. 5. ASPY may result in fewer unadjusted failures at day 42 compared to AL. This conclusion is based on data from 2,004 participants across three randomized controlled trials. The difference was estimated at 0 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 2 fewer to 11 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to very serious imprecision. 6. It is unclear whether there is a difference in the rate of serious adverse events between ASPY and AL. This conclusion is based on data from 3,415 participants across four randomized controlled trials. The difference was estimated at 7 more events per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 1 more to 22 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 7. ASPY may lead to a higher frequency of abnormal ALT increases compared to AL. This conclusion is based on data from 3,415 participants across four randomized controlled trials. The difference was estimated at 6 more events per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 1 more to 21 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 8. ASPY may lead to a higher frequency of abnormal AST increases compared to AL. This conclusion is based on data from trials conducted in Africa and Asia, which included both adults and children. However, only 115 children and no adults were randomized to ASPY in Asia. The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 9. Compared to AS-AQ, ASPY may result in fewer PCR-adjusted failures at day 28. This conclusion is based on data from 1,091 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 0 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 5 fewer to 23 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 10. There may be little or no difference in PCR-adjusted failures at day 42 between ASPY and AS-AQ. This conclusion is based on data from 1,257 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 38 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 52 fewer to 14 fewer). The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate due to serious indirectness. 11. ASPY probably results in fewer unadjusted failures at day 28 compared to AS-AQ. This conclusion is based on data from one study conducted at six sites in three West African countries. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate due to serious indirectness. 12. There is probably little or no difference in unadjusted failures at day 42 between ASPY and AS-AQ. This conclusion is based on data from 1,317 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 0 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 1 fewer to 6 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 13. ASPY may lead to a higher frequency of abnormal ALT increases compared to AS-AQ. This conclusion is based on data from 1,317 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 2 fewer events per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 4 fewer to 4 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and very serious imprecision. 14. It is unclear whether there is a difference in AST levels between ASPY and AS-AQ. This conclusion is based on data from 1,317 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 0 fewer events per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 1 fewer to 15 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and very serious imprecision. 15. It is unclear whether there is a difference in bilirubin levels between ASPY and AS-AQ. Serious adverse events data were not available in a disaggregated format to allow inclusion in this comparison. 16. Compared to MQ+AS, ASPY may result in fewer PCR-adjusted failures at day 28. This conclusion is based on data from 1,117 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 14 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 19 fewer to 1 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 17. ASPY may result in more PCR-adjusted failures at day 42 compared to MQ+AS. This conclusion is based on data from 1,037 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 23 more failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 3 fewer to 75 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 18. ASPY probably results in fewer unadjusted failures at day 28 compared to MQ+AS. This conclusion is based on data from 1,059 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 13 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 38 fewer to 26 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 19. There is probably little or no difference in unadjusted failures at day 42 between ASPY and MQ+AS. This conclusion is based on data from 1,271 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 0 fewer failures per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 0 fewer to 0 fewer). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to very serious imprecision and serious indirectness. 20. ASPY may lead to a higher frequency of abnormal ALT increases compared to MQ+AS. This conclusion is based on data from 1,271 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 5 more events per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 1 fewer to 55 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and very serious imprecision. 21. It is unclear whether there is a difference in AST levels between ASPY and MQ+AS. This conclusion is based on data from 1,271 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference was estimated at 0 fewer events per 1,000 participants (95% CI: 0 fewer to 0 fewer). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to very serious imprecision and serious indirectness. 22. It is unclear whether there is a difference in bilirubin levels between ASPY and MQ+AS. Serious adverse events data were not available in a disaggregated format to allow inclusion in this comparison. 23. Across all antimalarial comparisons, ASPY may lead to a higher frequency of abnormal ALT and AST increases. However, the certainty of evidence remains low to very low due to serious indirectness and imprecision in the data. These findings are based on systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials conducted in various settings, including Africa and Asia, and include both adults and children. However, the limited number of participants in some regions and the variability in study designs contribute to the overall uncertainty of the evidence.
